reasoning: Sherwood notes that since budget day, income generation has become a dominant investor priority and he expects this to persist for 12-18 months. He sees both public wholesale bonds and private credit as strong contributors to the income component of investor portfolios.

headline: Credit spreads likely to widen as economy softens, higher base rates and wider spreads creating better risk-reward for new private credit investors
reasoning: Sherwood expects a general economic softening driven by persistent inflation, cost-of-living pressures, and further rate rises, all of which should push credit spreads wider. He also anticipates some capital leaving the private credit sector. Together these factors mean new investors deploying capital over the next six months should be able to negotiate stronger returns and tighter covenants, improving overall risk-reward compared to recent vintages.
quote: The irony, Andrew, is that now we're actually going to see better risk reward across most, most areas of the market. I think from a credit spread point of view, the tendency for credit spreads, they should be widening and they probably highly likely will widen from here, particularly if we're entering a general softening in the economy. There's no doubt about that. More rate rises are needed. The cost of living keeps going up. Inflation is not getting under control. All of these components speak to a general economic softening. And that actually should push credit spreads a little wider. So you're going to have higher base rates and you're going to have slightly wider credit spreads. And maybe just a little bit of capital coming out of the sector as well, from a private credit lens point of view, will actually mean that risk reward on new trades for people who have money to put to work will actually be more favorable towards the investor, i.e. you can negotiate for a stronger return and maybe stronger covenants on your loans that you're providing.

headline: Not all private credit is equal — construction is inherently riskier; diversification across corporate, asset-backed and property sub-sectors is key to managing concentration risk
reasoning: Sherwood argues that recent high-profile collapses (e.g. Baffler in NSW) are not a new phenomenon but rather highlight the dangers of concentration in property-related private credit, which represents roughly 60% of Australian private credit. He distinguishes between riskier construction-focused lending and lower-risk corporate and asset-backed credit. His firm runs roughly one-third allocations across corporate, asset-backed and property, and has largely avoided construction risk. He stresses that manager selection and diversification are the primary mitigants.
quote: I think all these headlines are really highlighting that not all private credit is equal, and it never has been. Construction risk has always been a riskier part of private credit. That is nothing new at all. But what has been really shown, I guess, in some of these headlines is that concentrations of exposures is risky. We don't have any exposure to Baffler. But we've largely avoided construction risk because we have seen some potential headwinds coming in in that sector. But I think also it highlights that selection of your manager is important. And also diversification is important. So, you know, a large percentage of private credit in Australia has been concentrated around property — about 60% of private credit in Australia is property related — whereas there is a lot of other areas of private credit available as well through corporate credit, through asset backed credit.
episode_title: How to mitigate risk in private credit

headline: iPartners sees Australian property market remaining soft through end of 2025, with potential floor forming in early 2027 as rate cut expectations build
reasoning: Mark Sherwood expects the property market downturn to continue softening through to the end of 2025. He notes that markets may start pricing in a rate cut in the second half of 2026, which could put a floor under property prices around early 2027. He also flags that valuations in the sector have not yet fully reflected the current softness, suggesting more pain may be ahead before stabilisation.
quote: We do see it continuing to be softer right through to the end of this year. That said, wouldn't be at all surprised that the market actually starts focusing on the potential for a rate cut maybe in the second half of of next year. So that probably puts some sort of flaw in property prices, maybe at the, you know, the start of, of 2027, in our eyes, in terms of what's going on right now, I would say that we probably haven't quite seen the softness coming through in valuations.
episode_title: How the property downturn is reshaping private credit

headline: iPartners tightening focus to first mortgage lending only and increasing valuation scrutiny amid property market softness
reasoning: In the current softer property environment, iPartners has maintained a strict preference for first mortgage lending and has avoided second mortgage deals entirely. Sherwood emphasises the need to be more selective and rigorous around valuations, including verifying the quality of the valuation firm and seeking second or third opinions where warranted. He frames this as taking existing prudent practices to a higher level given the current environment.
quote: We're really trying to keep a preference towards first mortgage lending. We haven't really done anything in terms of a second mortgage type deal in this in this softer environment. So I would say our preference just a first mortgage exposed, uh, only in terms of in private credit. And we're very mindful of, of valuations and, and being very selective, I would say, in whether we're comfortable with the valuation before we go ahead and, and and do any type of deal.

headline: iPartners sees improved risk-reward in private credit as competition thins and credit spreads widen, marking a potential inflection point
reasoning: Sherwood notes that the private credit sector has seen some capital outflows over the past six months, driven by negative headlines both domestically and globally. This has led to reduced competition when negotiating deals and slightly wider outright yields. He characterises the current environment as a juncture point where the risk-reward profile has tilted more favourably compared to 12 months ago, suggesting the setup is actually better for disciplined lenders like iPartners.
quote: We've also seen a little bit of credit spread widening generally. So interestingly we're seeing I would say less a little bit less competition when negotiating on potential trades right now. And we're seeing a little bit wider outright yields on the back of on the back of both those factors, a little bit less money in the sector and a little bit wider on the credit spread. So if anything from a risk reward point of view, we're probably at a bit of a juncture point where where the risk reward is actually tilting a little bit more favorable amongst a little bit less competition than what there was in the sector 12 months ago.

headline: iPartners' Mark Sherwood sees strong diversification and income benefits in professionally managed private credit portfolios, favouring low-risk, stable-earnings businesses
reasoning: Sherwood argues that much of the public discourse around private credit focuses disproportionately on risks while ignoring the large volume of successful transactions. He emphasises that private credit can target businesses with very stable, consistent earnings that are not subject to swings in consumer spending and can be recession-proof. For retail investors and financial planners who lack deal-by-deal analytical capability, he recommends a diversified, professionally managed private credit fund with 50-60 underlying positions as the best risk-reward profile. He also highlights consistent monthly or quarterly income distributions as a key attraction of the asset class.
quote: I think when you think about risk in private credit, and this probably gets missed a little bit in the um, in a lot of the discussion and talk and papers is, yes, you can fund some, some really high risk businesses, but you can find some really, really low risk businesses, businesses that have very stable, consistent earnings profiles. And that's the kind of business that, uh, that we're looking for when we when we look for a private credit opportunity, businesses that are that are robust, um, their earnings are not subject to swings in consumer spending habits. Uh, and these sort of businesses can be quite recession proof as well.
episode_title: How to diversify your portfolio in a slowing economy
